tldr: To stitch together useful behaviors from imperfect demonstrations and failed trials, this work directly bridges high-dimensional image observations with physically plausible actions using a local inverse dynamics model and a reachability verifier, significantly boosting success rates on real-robot tasks.
hero_caption: Overview of offline dataset rewriting with Needle. It realizes three types of bridges: shortcuts that bypass inefficient detours within the same trajectory (S1), transplants that connect different successful trajectories to find better procedures (S2), and funnels that rescue failed episodes as useful starting behaviors and merge them into successful trajectories (S3).
overview:
When collecting robot demonstration data, not every episode turns out perfect. Even trials with unnecessary detours or failures in later stages contain highly valuable partial behaviors. Trajectory stitching—composing these pieces into ideal training data—has long been studied. However, most prior methods rely on low-dimensional simulator states, accurate global dynamics models, or task-wide value functions, making them extremely difficult to apply to high-dimensional, unstructured real-robot setups centered on camera images.

Needle (NEEDLEWORK) addresses this challenge by framing the issue as a short-horizon local reachability problem. Using only images and proprioception as input, it generates short action sequences transitioning from one observation to another via a goal-conditioned diffusion inverse dynamics model (IDM). Furthermore, an independently trained action-conditioned verifier checks whether the action actually reaches the target state, selecting only physically feasible bridges.

From collected datasets, Needle extracts candidates that achieve detour shortening, smooth transitions into better trajectories, and recovery from failed trials into successful ones, incorporating them into imitation learning training data without synthesizing intermediate images. Evaluated on real dual-arm tasks such as sweater folding and dish racking, as well as various simulation benchmarks, Needle improved real-robot success rates by an average of 21 percentage points over the strongest baseline, demonstrating a powerful framework for making full use of existing robot data without discarding it.
contributions: Proposed Needle, an offline data-augmentation method that uses only images and proprioception to generate and filter physically plausible action bridges via a local inverse dynamics model (IDM) and a reachability verifier.

Defined three bridging strategies—shortcutting detours, transplanting across trajectories, and funneling failed episodes—identifying useful connections based on time-to-reach reduction criteria without task value functions or privileged state.

Constructed a sliding-window sampling design that trains policies without synthesizing intermediate images, avoiding coordinate frame mismatches while preserving the original dataset's action coverage.
Demonstrated an average 21 percentage point improvement in success rate over conventional imitation learning and data-curation baselines on real dual-arm manipulation tasks.

sections.heading: Crafting perfect data by stitching: Trajectory stitching on high-dimensional images
sections.summary: Robot demonstration data often contains inefficient motions and failures, but stitching them together can produce a dataset superior to any single trajectory. This paper introduces Needle, a trajectory stitching method that avoids global models by decomposing the challenge into local reachability verification, functioning reliably even on image-based real-robot data.
sections.details:
In robot manipulation learning, collecting flawless demonstrations in a single run is difficult. For instance, in dual-arm sweater folding, one trial might fold the sleeves neatly but struggle with the hem, while another folds the hem cleanly after a clumsy sleeve fold. If we could stitch together the best parts of both, we could create a demonstration of higher quality than either trial alone.

Stitching trajectories together offers three major advantages:
- Intra-trajectory shortcuts: Bypassing useless detours and hesitations within the same episode to teach the shortest route.
- Inter-trajectory transplants: Connecting the strong phases of separate successful trajectories to synthesize efficient procedures never recorded directly.
- Rescuing failed trajectories: Merging intermediate states of failed episodes back into successful trajectories, repurposing them as recovery behaviors.

However, realizing this on high-dimensional real-robot observations (RGB images) was previously difficult. A connection must be both useful for the task and physically reachable (executable). Most existing approaches rely on low-dimensional privileged states or precise simulator transitions, or they merely filter and reweight existing data without supplying the missing physical actions needed to link desirable states.

To tackle this, the authors stepped away from learning global transition models or long-horizon value functions, reframing the challenge as a few-step local reachability problem. Short recorded transitions in the data serve as direct ground-truth supervision for which observations are reachable from one another, with what actions, and in how many steps. Leveraging this insight, they separately train an inverse dynamics model (IDM) to propose candidate actions and a verifier to scrutinize them.

captions.F1: Figure 1: Concept of Needle. Given original data (left) with inefficient detours, narrow success coverage, and discarded failure trajectories, Needle sews verified local bridges (green lines, right) to reconstruct high-quality, broad training data offline.

sections.heading: How does it compare to prior work? Explicit synthesis, data curation, and offline RL
sections.summary: Existing offline data augmentation methods roughly fall into low-dimensional trajectory stitching, importance weighting and filtering, or value propagation via offline reinforcement learning. Needle sets itself apart by explicitly synthesizing executable action bridges offline and incorporating them into imitation learning without requiring image synthesis or heavy inference-time search.
sections.details:
To clarify its position, related work is organized into three main categories:

### Explicit offline trajectory stitching
Methods that directly link trajectories to create new training data. However, most prior studies assume low-dimensional state representations or privileged simulator environments. When applied to images, they typically require generative models to synthesize intermediate frames. Needle generates no intermediate images at all, connecting recorded real observations solely through action sequences and avoiding the hallucinations and geometric inconsistencies common in image generation.

### Data curation (filtering, retrieval, and reweighting)
Approaches like SBR or SARM extract only the good portions from mixed-quality datasets. While they can re-evaluate beneficial transitions from failed episodes or low-quality demos, they do not rewrite the recorded actions themselves. Consequently, they cannot provide new actions to bridge distant states. Needle goes beyond filtering by generating the missing connecting actions.

### Implicit stitching and offline reinforcement learning
Q-learning and offline RL methods (such as IDQL) implicitly compose trajectories by propagating values through Bellman equations. However, learning value functions can be unstable under high-dimensional image observations and sparse reward setups. Moreover, some methods require complex policy guidance or trajectory search at test time. Because Needle rewrites the dataset offline beforehand, standard imitation learning policies like Diffusion Policy can be deployed at inference time with lightweight execution.

sections.heading: Teaming the needle and thimble: Action generation with IDM and verification via reachability
sections.summary: Needle determines a connection's usefulness by the reduction in remaining steps and guarantees its feasibility through the collaboration of an action generator (IDM) and a reachability verifier. Furthermore, it safely incorporates bridges into policy training using existing observations and a sliding window without synthesizing intermediate images.
sections.details:
In rewriting datasets, Needle sequentially answers two core questions: where to connect (usefulness) and whether it actually connects (feasibility).

### 3.1 Notation and basic definitions
A dataset $\mathcal{D}$ consists of trajectories of observations $o_t$, containing RGB images $x_t$ and proprioception $p_t$, paired with actions $a_t$. A starting observation is denoted as source $s$, and the destination as target $g$. A verified prefix of a generated action sequence is called a bridge, $b=(s, g, \hat{a}_{1:\ell})$.

### 3.2 Where should we connect? (Candidate selection)
Connecting nearby states indiscriminately risks creating unnecessary detours. Needle defines three candidate categories:
- S1 (Intra-trajectory shortcut): Shortcutting to a later state within the same successful trajectory.
- S2 (Inter-trajectory transplant): Switching to a state in another successful trajectory that has fewer remaining steps to the goal.
- S3 (Failure funnel): Merging an intermediate state from a failed trajectory into an appropriate state on a successful trajectory.

For connections between successful trajectories, a bridge is retained only if the step reduction $\Delta_{\mathrm{cont}}(b) = (T_i - t) - [\ell + (T_j - t')]$ is positive, where $(T_i - t)$ is the original remaining steps, $\ell$ is the bridge length, and $(T_j - t')$ is the remaining steps after the target. For each source, only the single most efficient bridge minimizing the total remaining steps $\ell + (T_j - t')$ is kept.

### 3.3 Training the needle and thimble (Decoupling generation and verification)
- Action Proposal (IDM): Implemented as a goal-conditioned diffusion inverse dynamics model. Given an observation pair $(s, g)$, it samples $K$ action candidates over horizon $H$. It trains on short intervals ($\delta \le H$) from the offline data, using target-pose hold padding if the target is reached early.
- Action Verifier: Checks whether the IDM's proposed action truly reaches $g$. Taking the source, goal, and proposed action sequence as input, it predicts the reachability probability $r_h$ at each step $h$ using causal attention. It trains via binary cross-entropy on a balanced mix of positive transitions, temporally distant negative pairs, and unrelated cross-trajectory negatives from the offline data, applying a strict threshold to suppress false positives.

### 3.4 Policy learning from stitches
Generated bridges lack intermediate images, and their endpoints may have slight reaching errors or coordinate frame mismatches relative to target observations. To handle this, Needle starts training windows $q$ steps prior to the bridge start point, using the concatenated sequence of "original recorded actions" followed by "bridge actions" as the learning target. Actions past the end of the bridge are masked out from the loss. This avoids forced image generation or discontinuous action jumps while preserving the state coverage of the original demonstrations.

captions.F2: Figure 2: Pipeline from candidate pairs to verified bridges. For candidate $(s,g)$, the IDM samples $K$ action proposals, and the verifier evaluates reaching probabilities at each step, adopting the shortest prefix that exceeds the threshold as the bridge.
captions.F3: Figure 3: Sliding window mechanism to train policies without intermediate images. Starting from an observation prior to the bridge, it chains original demo actions (light blue) and bridge actions (green). Actions beyond the bridge endpoint are masked out to avoid unnatural stitching, while subsequent target steps are trained separately with their original observations.

sections.heading: Real-world and simulation validation: A 21-point boost and behavioral shifts
sections.summary: On real dual-arm manipulation tasks and simulation benchmarks, Needle substantially outperformed existing imitation learning, data curation, and reinforcement learning baselines. Detailed analyses confirmed a dramatic reduction in wasteful hesitation, shorter task completion times, and superior recovery from failed states.
sections.details:
To evaluate the proposed method, extensive comparative experiments were conducted on both real robots and simulated environments.

### 4.1 Experimental setup
In the real-world setup, a dual-arm robot (ARX-5) was evaluated on Sweater Folding and Dish Racking using only RGB images and relative proprioception gathered via a handheld device (iPhUMI). In simulation, Robomimic Multi-Human datasets (Can, Square, and Transport) were used, comprising 40 suboptimal successful demonstrations and 150 failed rollouts. Comparisons were made against standard Diffusion Policy (DP), explicit stitching via MBTS, importance reweighting via AWR, data curation baselines SBR and SARM, and offline RL via IDQL.

### 4.2 Policy success rate improvements
On real-robot tasks, Needle exceeded the strongest baseline by 24 percentage points on Sweater Folding and 18 percentage points on Dish Racking, achieving an average 21 percentage point boost (Sweater Folding: 96%, Dish Racking: 88%). Baselines frequently suffered from cyclic, wasteful motions inherited from human demonstrations, such as repeatedly folding and unfolding sleeves or endlessly circling the rack with the gripper. Needle noticeably eliminated these detours. On Robomimic simulations, Needle also achieved an average improvement of 8.4 percentage points over DP and 6.9 percentage points over the strongest baseline.

### 4.3 How did learned behaviors change?
Analyses leveraging simulation reset capabilities revealed several key effects:
- Shorter completion steps: Comparing rollouts from the same state that either executed the original continuation or the bridge, traversing the bridge clearly reduced the remaining steps required to finish the task.
- Recovery from failures: Training data added via failure funnels extended into out-of-distribution (OOD) regions relative to original successful demonstrations. When intentionally restarted from failure states, Needle demonstrated far higher recovery rates than DP or AWR.

### 4.4 Is the verifier truly necessary?
When adopting IDM proposals directly without the verifier, the success rate on Transport plummeted from 53.2% to 20.4% (a 61.7% relative drop). This confirms that the verifier's ability to filter for high-precision actions reaching within 5 cm is vital to performance gains.

### 4.5 What happens when demonstrations are already near-optimal?
In experiments on DexMimicGen high-quality demonstrations, Needle's improvement plateaued at around 4 percentage points. The method's core value shines brightest when dealing with messy data containing inefficiencies and failures.

Right: Needle outperforms other methods in recovery success rate when restarted from these failure states.

sections.heading: Conclusion: Moving from curating demonstrations to stitching and creating them
sections.summary: Needle is a powerful approach for rewriting imperfect robot datasets offline directly within high-dimensional observation spaces. By decomposing the problem into local reachability rather than relying on global models, it demonstrates across real and simulated setups that practical policies can be learned from data filled with failures and detours.
sections.details:
This work introduced Needle, a data augmentation algorithm that recomposes useful behaviors from low-quality and failed offline robot demonstrations. Its key breakthrough lies in reducing the historical challenge of trajectory stitching in high-dimensional image spaces down to a manageable supervised learning problem: short-horizon local reachability verification.

Extensive real-world and simulation experiments verified that Needle reliably delivers three key benefits: bypassing detours, complementary composition across trajectories, and acquiring recovery behaviors from failed episodes.

The essential message of this paper is a paradigm shift in offline robot learning: rather than simply filtering, reweighting, or discarding data, we can actively synthesize entirely new, high-quality supervisory data by carefully stitching together existing behavioral fragments.

sections.heading: Appendix: Sampling techniques for training and in-depth ablation studies
sections.summary: The appendix details ablation studies on sampling designs used to safely integrate stitched data into policy training, analyzes the contribution of each connection stage (S1–S3), and provides tuning details for various baselines.
sections.details:
The appendix validates critical design choices complementing the main text.

### Ablation on training sampling (App. B.3)
The construction of bridge training windows was analyzed through several ablations:
- Discarding the original action at the bridge start point and training only on the bridge degraded performance. Keeping the original action preserves diverse choices for the policy.
- Completely removing data bypassed by shortcuts dropped the Transport success rate from 53.2% to 50.0%. Retaining observations and actions from bypassed regions contributes to policy robustness.
- Forcibly concatenating continuing actions from the target trajectory onto the end of the bridge degraded performance on Square (47.2% to 42.0%) and Transport (53.2% to 45.6%). Due to slight landing errors and coordinate frame shifts, Needle's design of masking past the bridge end and training continuations separately is essential.

### Importance of bridge actions themselves (App. B.4)
To prove gains did not simply stem from reweighting data sampling frequencies, policies were trained after removing all windows containing bridge actions. Success rates dropped sharply: Can fell from 83.6% to 77.2%, Square from 47.2% to 42.8%, and Transport from 53.2% to 45.6%. This confirms improvements stem directly from the generated action bridges.

### Contribution of each connection stage (App. B.2)
Investigating combinations of shortcuts (S1), transplants (S2), and funnels (S3) showed that no single stage achieved peak performance across all three tasks. In particular, adding S3 (failure recovery) provided a massive boost on Transport, jumping from 45.6% to 53.2%.

takeaways: Separating a local inverse dynamics model (IDM) from a reachability verifier enables safe, image-based trajectory stitching without relying on global value functions or image generation.
Failed episodes and detour-heavy demos do not need to be thrown away; connecting them to successful trajectories via local bridges transforms them into effective recovery data and shortcuts.

When incorporating synthesized action bridges into training, masking actions past the bridge endpoint rather than forcing continuous concatenation—while maintaining original data coverage—is key to preventing policy collapse.
limitations: When demonstrations are already near-optimal, there is little room for shortening or restructuring, resulting in marginal gains from Needle (only a few percentage points).

Tasks involving prolonged physical contact, transitions requiring significant object rearrangement along the way, or connections requiring dense closed-loop visual feedback during execution exceed the current fixed-horizon local bridge framework.
